newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Thousands protest as Belgians seethe over sex case.
newsitem.headline: Thousands protest as Belgians seethe over sex case.

text.p: Protesters pelted the Justice Palaces in Antwerp and Hasselt with stones.
There was a bomb scare at the Vilvoorde home of Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene.
And demonstrators in Turhout with pasta in their hair gave the public prosecutor dried spaghetti.

It was the third day of demonstrations in a wave of anger sweeping Belgium since magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte was removed from investigations into a child sex ring held responsible for killing at least four young girls.
Even bigger protests are expected on Sunday when marchers dressed in white and carrying white flowers will stream into Brussels from all over the country and abroad.

Thousands of students, factory workers, coach drivers and office staff on both sides of Belgium's linguistic divide took part in Thursday's displays of disgust with the country's legal system and rage at the treatment of Connerotte.
The magistrate was judged by the country's highest court to have compromised himself by accepting a plate of spaghetti at a dinner given by a group helping the parents of missing children.

Connerotte, whose job as an investigating magistrate is to build a balanced case file both for and against prosecution, has become a national hero for his running of enquiries into the paedophile ring led by convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux.

Belgium has been reeling from shock since mid-August when two young sexually-abused girls were rescued from a secret dungeon in a house owned by Dutroux, followed by the discovery of the dead bodies of four others missing for over a year.
There have been revelations of past police and judicial bungling, fuelling suspicions of a high level cover-up.
So far 13 people have been charged in relation to the investigations, and a team of more than 350 police are on the case and still seeking at least seven other missing children.
Police and Brussels administration officials are bracing for action at a mass rally on Sunday organised by the parents of some of the dead and missing children.
Paul Marchal, father of one of the dead girls, An, appealed to the crowd in his home town of Hasselt for calm during Sunday's rally at which police unofficially expect upwards of 100,000 people.
But his brother-in-law told VTM television he feared things could get out of hand.
Deputy Brussels Mayor Freddy Thielemans told a news conference there would be 400 police and 1,000 gendarmes on duty on Sunday who would be ready to stamp out any violent incidents.
But he said he did not believe there would be any because it would be an insult to the memories of the dead and missing children and would not be tolerated by the public themselves.
"We would like to see the march going on in calm and with dignity," he said. "That is the way to respect the victims."
Belgian railways is offering subsidised tickets and putting on extra trains, and Thielemans said all of the buses and coaches in the provinces of Flanders and Liege had been booked for Sunday.

Police are setting up free parking areas on the outskirts of Brussels and laying on free bus services to the Gare du Nord starting point and from the Gare du Midi end point in what one observer dubbed a "park and march" exercise. It is due to rain.
